keyTakeaways: मुझे भी तुम्हारी याद आ रही है for someone you call tum; swap तुम्हारी for आपकी for an elder — Platts tags आप as a reverential pronoun.
Move भी from मुझे to तुम्हारी and 'I miss you too' becomes 'I miss you as well as other people'. The particle attaches to the word before it.
The page ranking #2 on Google India offers मैं भी तुम्हें याद करता हूँ as 'I miss you, too', but याद करना carries no 'miss' sense in Wiktionary or in Platts p. 1247.
Replying in English is normal, not cold: across 1,828 clauses from younger Hindi speakers, Klingler (2017) found them alternating between fully English and fully Hindi clauses as a matter of course.
Across 214 miss-you pages, recipients tapped a hug 1,434 times on 138 of them — the commonest reply we can see is not a sentence at all.

faqs.question: Miss you ka reply kya de in one line?
faqs.answer: मुझे भी तुम्हारी याद आ रही है (mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai) for anyone you call tum, and मुझे भी आपकी याद आ रही है (mujhe bhi aapki yaad aa rahi hai) for an elder. Swap तुम्हारी for आपकी and you have changed the whole social level of the message.

faqs.question: Is main bhi or mujhe bhi correct?
faqs.answer: Both are used. मुझे भी matches the Hindi construction, because याद आना takes a dative experiencer — मुझे — and has no first-person subject. मैं भी matches the English sentence, which does have an I. If the message you received was in Hindi, मुझे भी continues it properly.

faqs.question: Can I just reply in English?
faqs.answer: Yes, and there is no evidence it reads as cold. Klingler's 2017 recordings in Dehradun found younger Hindi speakers alternating between fully English and fully Hindi clauses as a matter of course, across 1,828 clauses. Matching whatever they sent is the safest read.

faqs.question: What does yaad karna mean, and why is it wrong here?
faqs.answer: Wiktionary glosses याद करना only as 'to remember, to recall'. Platts adds 'to commit to memory' and 'to send for, to require the presence of (a subordinate)'. None of those is 'to miss'. The miss sense belongs to याद आना, which is why मैं तुम्हें याद करता हूँ does not say what people think it says.

faqs.question: What is the difference between mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai and mujhe tumhari bhi yaad aa rahi hai?
faqs.answer: The first means 'I miss you too'. The second means 'I miss you as well as other people'. भी attaches to whatever comes immediately before it, so moving it from मुझे to तुम्हारी turns a warm reply into an accidental list.

faqs.question: Can I say mujhe bhi teri yaad aa rahi hai to my girlfriend?
faqs.answer: Only if तू is already how you speak to each other. Wiktionary notes that in the Hindi-Urdu Belt तू is chiefly used insultingly, while in Maharashtra it is normal between spouses, siblings and friends. It is the most intimate form and the easiest to get wrong.

faqs.question: Is hum bhi wrong Hindi?
faqs.answer: No. Wiktionary records हम as a first-person singular meaning 'I' in Varanasi and Awadh, and notes that most Eastern Hindi dialects use हम only for 'I'. It is regional, not incorrect — it will simply sound eastern to a Delhi reader.

faqs.question: How do I reply to miss you from a parent or an older relative?
faqs.answer: Use आप: मुझे भी आपकी याद आ रही है. Platts tags आप as a reverential pronoun — 'You, Sir, your honour' — and Wiktionary calls it the safest default. Dropping to तुम or तू with an elder is the error people actually notice.

faqs.question: What do I say if I do not want to say it back?
faqs.answer: याद तो आती है (yaad to aati hai) is honest and carries no pronoun at all, so you avoid committing to a register as well as to a feeling. It says the memory comes, without saying who you are to each other now.

faqs.question: Should I write the reply in Devanagari or in Roman letters?
faqs.answer: Match what they sent. Roman Hindi is how most people actually type, and none of the grammar above changes — bhi still attaches to the word before it, and teri, tumhari and aapki still carry their registers, script or no script.

faqs.question: Is replying with just a heart or an emoji enough?
faqs.answer: It is a real reply and often the right one. On our own 214 miss-you pages, recipients tapped a hug 1,434 times across 138 pages rather than typing anything, so a non-verbal answer is the commonest response we can actually see.

faqs.question: How long should the reply be?
faqs.answer: Shorter than you think. The median letter people write on our miss-you template is 88 words and the longest is 1,024, but that is for something built over a median 2.6 hours. A chat reply is one sentence plus one specific detail.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Miss You Ka Reply Kya De: The Hindi Answer, Register by Register

**Miss you ka reply kya de?** *Mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai* (मुझे भी तुम्हारी याद आ रही है) for anyone you call *tum*; *mujhe bhi aapki yaad aa rahi hai* (मुझे भी आपकी याद आ रही है) for an elder. The trap: "miss you" arrived in English, which commits you to nothing, and Hindi will not let you answer without picking a register.

Two numbers from our own data first. Across 214 "I miss you" pages built on SubhSandesh since 2026-07-28, recipients have tapped a hug **1,434 times across 138 of the 214 pages** — 64.5% got at least one, 512 taps on one page. The median gap between a sender's first save and last edit is **2.6 hours, n=214**.

They take an afternoon over what they send you; you get nine seconds to answer. The question is not which line is sweetest, but which is correct for this person.

## What actually ranks for this query in India

Measured 2026-09-27 on Google served to India, `gl=in&hl=en&pws=0`, in a real browser. Nine results were read; ranks past that are not reported, because they were not seen.
Four of the nine are YouTube videos, the top one a 45-second clip with 213,000 views. One is hi.wikiHow, machine-translated from English. One is a Quora thread answering "We miss you", a different question. One is Reddit behind Google's Hindi-Latin translation layer; the last two are Preply and a US listicle. **Eight of the nine are weak.**

Brave with `country=in` is worse: eight results are `translate.google.com` URLs wrapping English pages, and both real Hindi blogs are dead. `theindianposts.co.in` returns NXDOMAIN; `hindimeg.net/i-miss-you-ka-reply-kya-hoga/` now serves an Indonesian gambling storefront, "HWGSLOT Dengan Angka Togel Resmi", with zero occurrences of याद on it.

The SERP is English answers pushed through a translator. Nobody chose the register.

## The reply everyone types first, and what it actually says

The reflex is *main bhi* (मैं भी) or *mujhe bhi* (मुझे भी). Both are used; they are not the same move.

Hindi does not say "I miss you" with "I" as the subject. The verb is **याद आना**, *yād ānā*, which Wiktionary glosses "to miss, long for" with the example `तुम्हारी बहुत याद आ रही है।` — "I miss you a lot." Platts, page 1247 of his 1884 dictionary, gives it as "To come to recollection or mind; to recur to memory." The memory is the grammatical subject; you are the dative experiencer, मुझे.

So **मुझे भी** echoes the Hindi sentence and **मैं भी** echoes the English one, which does have an "I". Neither is an error — but *main bhi* cannot be expanded into a Hindi sentence built on याद आना, so if the message was in Hindi, *mujhe bhi* is the one that continues it.

## The mistake on the page ranking second

hi.wikiHow sits at position two with 54,004 views. Its Method 1 of 15 is `"क्या बात है! मैं भी तुम्हें याद करता हूँ!"`, glossed by the page itself as *"What a coincidence! I miss you, too!"*. Method 14 uses the same verb.

Both are built on **याद करना**, not याद आना. Wiktionary gives याद करना one sense, "to remember, to recall" — no 'miss' sense. Platts is blunter: *yād karnā* is "To think of, to remember, recollect, call to mind; — to commit to memory; — **to send for, to require the presence of (a subordinate)**."

So the most-read Hindi reply on this SERP, offered as "I miss you, too", is glossed by both dictionaries as "I remember you too". On that page `याद कर` appears 13 times and `याद आ` three — a calque, which is what a translated page produces.

## Where *bhi* goes decides who you are talking about

*Bhi* is a focus particle. Platts, page 198, glosses भी "Also, too, even… likewise, moreover, furthermore." Wiktionary shows what that means: `तुम भी जाओगी?` is "Will **you too** go?" The particle attaches to whatever sits immediately before it — and a 2024 study of Bollywood dialogue in *English Language and Linguistics* quotes the same pattern from *Dear Zindagi*: `hum easy option bhī choose kar sakte hɛ̃ nā`, "we can **also** choose an easy option".

Two replies, three characters apart. *Mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai* — मुझे **भी** — is "I miss you too": you are the one being added.

*Mujhe tumhari bhi yaad aa rahi hai* — तुम्हारी **भी** — is "I miss you **as well as the other people I am missing**." Sent to a partner it lands badly, and they will not be able to say why.

## तू, तुम, आप or हम — the choice English never made you make

"Miss you" is register-neutral. Your reply cannot be. Tatoeba's Hindi corpus shows it: `याद आ रही` returns exactly two sentences, `मुझें तुम्हारी याद आ रही है।` and `मुझें आपकी याद आ रही है।`, and **both are translated "I miss you."** One English sentence, two Hindi ones; the difference is entirely social.

- **आप** — *mujhe bhi aapki yaad aa rahi hai*. Platts tags आप "pron. rever. You, Sir, your honour"; Wiktionary calls it the most formal, "used when addressing elders or those higher in social status". A parent, a teacher, in-laws.
- **तुम** — *mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai*. Wiktionary: "mid-level formality and grammatically plural". A friend, a sibling, a partner. The one most readers want.
- **तू** — *mujhe bhi teri yaad aa rahi hai*. Wiktionary warns that in the Hindi–Urdu Belt तू is "chiefly used insultingly" and "the most common pronoun used in abusive or vulgar contexts", while in Maharashtra it is "normally used inoffensively… among social equals such as siblings, friends, and spouses".
- **हम भी** is not a mistake. Wiktionary gives हम a second sense beside "we" — "(Varanasi, Awadh, colloquial in Standard Hindi) I" — noting most Eastern Hindi dialects use it only for "I". It reads as regional in Delhi.

These are dictionary register labels, not usage data. I looked for a study of who Hindi speakers actually address as तू today and found none that is open.

## Is replying in English actually cold?

Probably not — but the evidence is thinner than anyone writing about this admits.

Klingler's 2017 study in *Lifespans and Styles* recorded 2 hours 7 minutes of conversation among six female Hindi speakers in Dehradun — three aged 54 to 63, three aged 24 to 35 — across 2,020 clauses from the older group and 1,828 from the younger. Younger speakers **alternate between fully Hindi and fully English clauses**; older speakers **insert English items into Hindi clauses**, and those insertions are overwhelmingly nouns: 69% and 71% in two older conversations, 74%, 51% and 76% in the three younger.

"Miss you" is a verb phrase, not a noun. A whole English clause arriving alone is the younger pattern, so answering in English matches it. From a parent it is likelier a stray English item inside a Hindi conversation, and a Hindi sentence back fits better.

The Bollywood study quotes Dwyer: English "has encroached little into the films themselves, although there are key stock phrases, such as saying *I love you*". The English affection formula inside Hindi speech is documented, not a lapse.

**Neither study measures warmth.** *Emotion*, *affect* and *intimacy* appear zero times in the Bollywood paper's full text. I searched five ways for research on whether an English reply reads colder to a Hindi–English bilingual and found nothing open-access and topical. No study says English is cold, and none says it isn't.

## Sort by who sent it, not by how it sounds

Most reply lists are wrong for most readers: a partner, a friend, an ex and a parent are four different messages sorted by tone into one list.

| Who sent it | Reply | Register | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Partner | मुझे भी तुम्हारी याद आ रही है (*mujhe bhi tumhari yaad aa rahi hai*) | तुम, mid | Add a concrete detail — our median miss-you letter is 88 words, the longest 1,024 |
| Close friend | मैं भी यार, बहुत (*main bhi yaar, bahut*) | तुम + vocative | The English-subject echo is fine, and a vocative lowers the register |
| Parent or elder | मुझे भी आपकी याद आ रही है (*mujhe bhi aapki yaad aa rahi hai*) | आप, reverential | Platts tags आप "pron. rever."; never तू upward |
| An ex, meaning nothing by it | याद तो आती है (*yaad to aati hai*) | pronoun-free | No register at all; 43.5% of our miss-you senders password-protect first |

## What our numbers can and cannot tell you

Every figure above comes from 214 pages on one template — 4.1% of the 5,221 pages we hold across 44 collections — built since 2026-07-28. Two months, one product: no seasonal claim survives that.

Recorded views are page views, not unique visitors. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not evidence of anyone's choice, which is why none appears here. And the limit that matters most: **our database records which template was opened, never who received it, and nothing is segmented by language or country.** The 1,434 hug taps prove a reply happened; they cannot say in what language.

**A reply is also a different job from building a page**, and nobody answers "miss you" with a link. When the sentence is genuinely not enough, our [I-miss-you page built for a partner](/missyou-gf) is the long form — built for a girlfriend or partner, with English labels, so it is the wrong object for a friend, a sibling or a parent. For a friend in another city, [the daily streak page](/streak) fits better, for the reason this post exists: **a tap has no register.** Otherwise, the [other templates](/templates).

If your question was how you feel rather than how to phrase it, our guide to [what to reply when someone says "I miss you"](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/what-to-reply-when-someone-says-i-miss-you) sorts by situation instead of register, and [miss you yaar meaning in Hindi](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/miss-you-yaar-meaning-in-hindi) handles the word this page left alone.

## Sources

- Platts, *A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English*, 1884: [*yād*, p. 1247](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=y%C4%81d&searchhws=yes), [*bhī*, p. 198](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=bh%C4%AB&searchhws=yes).
- Wiktionary, Hindi [याद आना](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A6_%E0%A4%86%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BE), with याद करना, भी, तू, तुम, आप, हम.
- [Tatoeba #2060321](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/2060321) and #2060322.
- Cowie, Murty & Sinar, "Decoding Bollywood", [*English Language and Linguistics* 28(4)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/EE5E177FA532B9FCB4DF32EDAFBC8D12/S1360674324000534a.pdf/div-class-title-decoding-bollywood-why-hindi-english-code-switching-and-standard-english-outrank-indian-english-div.pdf), CUP, 2024. Full text read.
- Klingler, "Changes in Code-Switching Patterns among Hindi-English Bilinguals in Northern India", [*Lifespans and Styles* 3(1)](https://journals.ed.ac.uk/lifespansstyles/article/view/1827), Edinburgh, 2017. Full text read.

THE REGISTER LADDER RESTS ON DICTIONARY LABELS, NOT USAGE DATA. Platts and Wiktionary say what तू, तुम and आप mean and how they are marked; neither is a study of who Indian speakers actually address as तू in 2026. The one topical politeness paper, 'Conventionalized Politeness Structures: Empirical Evidence from Hindi/Urdu' (Journal of Politeness Research, 2017, doi 10.1515/pr-2015-0001), is closed access — Unpaywall is_oa:false. Closes if that paper opens or an OA replication appears. The body prose says this rather than hiding it.

NO STUDY MEASURES WHETHER AN ENGLISH REPLY READS AS COLD. Five search phrasings returned nothing topical and open-access. The Bollywood paper contains 'emotion', 'affect' and 'intimac' zero times across 11,840 words of full text. The post reports this as a negative finding instead of stretching either source into an emotional claim.

THE CODE-SWITCHING EVIDENCE IS THIN BY THE AUTHORS' OWN ACCOUNT. Klingler (2017) is six speakers, all female, one city, one social class, recorded in 2012. Cowie et al. describe their own work as 'an exploratory and qualitative study, rather than compile a film corpus'. Both are cited with those limits stated in the body, and no per-group rate is derived from either.

FIRST-PARTY DIFFERENTIATION IS THIN. The 1,434-hug-tap line is also the lead fact of the live sibling what-to-reply-when-someone-says-i-miss-you, and the six miss-you lines in facts-snapshot.md are each carried by 48–63 posts across this batch and the last. The framing is new — a nine-second reply measured against a 2.6-hour composition window — but the numbers are shared, and no figure here is segmented by language or country because the database has no such segment.

THE PRODUCT IS THE WRONG SHAPE FOR THREE OF THE FOUR SENDERS THIS POST SORTS BY. /missyou-gf is defined at app/lib/prompt.ts:44 as an 'I miss you page for a girlfriend/partner'. For a friend, a sibling or a parent it is recipient-wrong, and its labels are in English. Disclosed in body prose. /streak is offered as the genuine alternative for the stated reason that a daily tap carries no register at all, which is the exact problem this post is about — and the body also names the larger tension, that a reply is a different job from building a page.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine asked 'miss you ka reply kya de' has, today, nothing to cite: four YouTube videos, a machine-translated wikiHow whose headline reply uses a verb no dictionary glosses as 'miss', a Quora thread about a different question, and eight Google-Translate proxies of American advice blogs. This page is the only one that decides the register — आप for an elder, तुम for a peer, तू at your own risk — and the only one that explains why moving भी by one word turns 'I miss you too' into 'I miss you as well as other people', each claim pinned to a named dictionary entry that was fetched and read. What it cannot do is beat domain authority: subhsandesh.in has 81 live pages in this cluster but no measured position on this query, hi.wikiHow has a decade of authority, and four of the nine slots are video, which a blog post cannot take. Ranking takes months and this post does not predict one. The weakest part is the first-party data: those six miss-you lines are shared with 48–63 sibling posts, and nothing in the database is segmented by language, so the numbers support the page rather than distinguishing it. The linguistic verification is what distinguishes it.
